baryon-number-minus-lepton-number-conser.title: Baryon Number Minus Lepton Number Conservation
baryon-number-minus-lepton-number-conser.conceptual_definition: The formula B - L = constant expresses a fundamental conservation law in particle physics. It states that the difference between the total baryon number (\(B\)) and the total lepton number (\(L\)) of a system remains invariant over time, provided that only interactions conserving both baryon and lepton numbers individually occur, or interactions that conserve their difference. This conservation law is crucial for understanding the behavior of elementary particles in various physical processes, from nuclear reactions to the early universe.
baryon-number-minus-lepton-number-conser.intuitive_summary: The imbalance between the count of matter particles made of quarks (baryons) and matter particles made of leptons never changes in interactions.
baryon-number-minus-lepton-number-conser.interpretation: In the equation \(B - L = \text{const}\), the symbol \(B\) represents the total baryon number of a system, and \(L\) represents the total lepton number. Baryons are composite particles made of three quarks (e.g., protons and neutrons), and each baryon is assigned a baryon number of \(+1\), while antibaryons have \(-1\). Quarks and antiquarks themselves also carry baryon numbers of \(+1/3\) and \(-1/3\) respectively, such that the net baryon number of a hadron is an integer. Leptons are elementary particles that do not interact via the strong nuclear force (e.g., electrons, muons, neutrinos), and each lepton is assigned a lepton number of \(+1\), while antileptons have \(-1\). The equation posits that in any physical process, the initial sum of \(B - L\) for all participating particles must equal the final sum of \(B - L\) for all resultant particles. This implies that while baryon number and lepton number can change individually in some speculative theories beyond the Standard Model (like proton decay), their difference is a more robust conserved quantity under a broader range of conditions.
baryon-number-minus-lepton-number-conser.symmetry_origin: The conservation of baryon number and lepton number are believed to be consequences of certain symmetries in the fundamental laws of physics, specifically related to gauge symmetries associated with the U(1) global symmetries of the Standard Model for each conserved quantity. However, the conservation of \(B-L\) is not a fundamental symmetry of the Standard Model itself, as processes like neutrino oscillations (which conserve \(B\) and \(L\) separately) do not violate \(B-L\). The conservation of \(B-L\) arises from the fact that the Standard Model interactions conserve both \(B\) and \(L\) individually. However, extensions to the Standard Model, such as Grand Unified Theories (GUTs), can contain interactions that violate both \(B\) and \(L\) but conserve their difference. For example, the decay of a proton into a positron and a neutral pion involves a change in both \(B\) and \(L\), but the difference \(B-L\) remains constant.
baryon-number-minus-lepton-number-conser.limits_and_boundary: In the limit where the number of baryons and leptons in a system are both negligible (approaching zero, i.e., a vacuum state or a system with only massless bosons not carrying baryon or lepton number), the difference \(B - L\) is zero and remains zero. As the number of baryons and leptons become very large, the conservation of \(B - L\) dictates the ratios and types of interactions that can occur. For instance, in extreme conditions like the early universe, the vast numbers of particles involved mean that any deviation from \(B - L\) conservation would have had observable cosmological consequences. In the context of specific particle interactions, if a process involves only particles with zero baryon and lepton numbers (like photon interactions), then \(B - L\) is trivially conserved at zero.

rotation-transformation.title: Rotation transformation
rotation-transformation.conceptual_definition: The formula \(\mathbf{r}' = \boldsymbol{R}\boldsymbol{r}\) describes how the coordinates of a point in space, represented by a vector \(\mathbf{r}\), are transformed to a new set of coordinates, \(\mathbf{r}'\), when the coordinate system undergoes a rotation. The matrix \(\boldsymbol{R}\) encapsulates the specific rotation applied, determining the orientation of the new coordinate system relative to the original one. This is fundamental in fields like classical mechanics, quantum mechanics, and computer graphics for managing objects and observers in three-dimensional space.
rotation-transformation.intuitive_summary: This equation mathematically expresses a rotation of a spatial vector by applying a rotation matrix to it.
rotation-transformation.interpretation: In this equation, \(\mathbf{r}\) represents the position vector of a point in an initial coordinate system. It is typically a column vector with components (e.g., \(x, y, z\)) in 3D space. The symbol \(\mathbf{r}'\) denotes the position vector of the same point but expressed in a *rotated* coordinate system. The core of the transformation is the matrix \(\boldsymbol{R}\), which is known as the rotation matrix. This matrix is a square matrix (e.g., 3x3 for 3D space) whose elements are determined by the angle and axis of rotation. When the rotation matrix \(\boldsymbol{R}\) is multiplied by the original position vector \(\mathbf{r}\) (matrix multiplication), the result is the new position vector \(\mathbf{r}'\) in the rotated frame. The dimensions of the vectors and the matrix must be compatible for the multiplication to be defined. If \(\mathbf{r}\) and \(\mathbf{r}'\) are n-dimensional vectors, then \(\boldsymbol{R}\) must be an n x n matrix. For a physical interpretation, \(\mathbf{r}\) and \(\mathbf{r}'\) typically have units of length (meters, m), and the rotation matrix \(\boldsymbol{R}\) is dimensionless, as it represents a geometric transformation.
rotation-transformation.symmetry_origin: This formula arises from the principles of coordinate transformations and the geometric properties of rotations. Rotations are a form of symmetry operation that preserve distances and angles, meaning the physical laws expressed in terms of such transformations should remain invariant under rotation. In physics, particularly in Lagrangian and Hamiltonian mechanics, conservation of angular momentum is directly linked to the invariance of physical systems under rotation (Noether's theorem). The rotation matrix \(\boldsymbol{R}\) can be derived from the fundamental properties of rotation, such as its orthogonality and determinant of 1.
rotation-transformation.limits_and_boundary: As the rotation angle approaches zero, the rotation matrix \(\boldsymbol{R}\) approaches the identity matrix. In this limit, \(\boldsymbol{R} 	o \boldsymbol{I}\), and thus \(\boldsymbol{r}' 	o \boldsymbol{I}\boldsymbol{r} = \boldsymbol{r}\), meaning the coordinates do not change, as expected for no rotation. For extreme rotations, such as rotations by multiples of \(2π\) radians (or 360 degrees), the rotation matrix returns to the identity matrix, implying the coordinate system is restored to its original orientation. The magnitude of the position vector \(\	ext{||}\boldsymbol{r}\	ext{||}\) remains invariant under rotation, so \(\	ext{||}\boldsymbol{r}'\	ext{||} = \	ext{||}\boldsymbol{r}\	ext{||}\) for any rotation \(\boldsymbol{R}\).

\\(\\mathbf{r}'\\).name: Transformed Position Vector
\\(\\mathbf{r}'\\).description: The position vector of a point after the coordinate system has been rotated. Its components are expressed in the new, rotated coordinate frame.

\\(\\boldsymbol{R}\\).name: Rotation Matrix
\\(\\boldsymbol{R}\\).description: A matrix that defines the specific rotation applied to the coordinate system. For a 3D rotation, it is a 3x3 orthogonal matrix with a determinant of 1. The elements of this matrix depend on the angle and axis of rotation.

\\(\\mathbf{r}\\).name: Original Position Vector
\\(\\mathbf{r}\\).description: The position vector of a point in the original, unrotated coordinate system. Its components are expressed in the initial frame.

ampere-law-free-current.title: Ampere's law with free current density
ampere-law-free-current.conceptual_definition: Ampere's law, in its form relating the magnetic field intensity \b{H} to the free current density \b{J}_f, is one of the fundamental equations of electromagnetism within Maxwell's equations. It describes how electric currents create magnetic fields. Specifically, it states that the circulation of the magnetic field intensity around any closed loop is proportional to the total free electric current passing through the surface enclosed by that loop. This form is particularly useful when dealing with situations where only free currents (e.g., conduction currents in wires) are present, and displacement currents or bound currents are negligible or absent.
ampere-law-free-current.intuitive_summary: The curl of the magnetic field intensity is directly equal to the free current density, meaning that circulating magnetic fields are produced by flowing electric charges.
ampere-law-free-current.interpretation: The equation \b{∇} \b{×} \b{H} = \b{J}_f relates the magnetic field intensity \b{H} to the free current density \b{J}_f. The left side, \b{∇} \b{×} \b{H}, represents the curl of the magnetic field intensity vector. The curl is a vector operator that describes how much a vector field 'rotates' or 'circulates' at a point. In this context, a non-zero curl of \b{H} signifies the presence of a magnetic field that is swirling around a certain region. The right side, \b{J}_f, is the free current density vector. Current density, measured in amperes per square meter (\b{A}/\b{m}^2), quantifies the amount of electric charge flowing per unit area per unit time. The 'free' designation distinguishes it from bound currents that arise from the magnetization of materials. This equation asserts that the spatial rate of change of the magnetic field intensity (its curl) at any point is precisely equal to the free electric current density flowing through that point. Therefore, flowing free electric charges are the source of circulating magnetic fields.
ampere-law-free-current.symmetry_origin: Ampere's Law is derived from the Biot-Savart Law and is fundamental to the description of magnetostatics. It can be expressed in integral form as \b{∮} \b{H} \b{⋅} \b{dl} = I_{f,enc}, which highlights that the line integral of \b{H} around a closed loop is proportional to the total free current enclosed. The differential form presented here (\b{∇} \b{×} \b{H} = \b{J}_f) is obtained by applying Stokes' theorem to the integral form. This equation reflects the fact that magnetic fields are generated by moving charges, and it is a key component of Maxwell's equations, which are Lorentz covariant and thus consistent with special relativity.
ampere-law-free-current.limits_and_boundary: In the absence of any free currents (\b{J}_f = 0), Ampere's law simplifies to \b{∇} \b{×} \b{H} = 0. This condition implies that the magnetic field intensity \b{H} is irrotational, meaning it can be expressed as the gradient of a scalar potential (\b{H} = -\b{∇}Φ_m, where Φ_m is the magnetic scalar potential). This is analogous to the electrostatic case where \b{∇} \b{×} \b{E} = 0 implies \b{E} = -\b{∇}Φ_e. Conversely, in regions with a very high free current density (\b{|J}_f| 	o \b{∞}), the curl of the magnetic field intensity will be correspondingly large, indicating strong circulating magnetic fields.

∇ × H.name: Curl of Magnetic Field Intensity
∇ × H.description: The curl of the magnetic field intensity vector, representing the circulation of the magnetic field at a point. In SI units, the curl of H has units of A/m^2.

J_f.name: Free Current Density
J_f.description: The density of free electric current flowing through a material, representing the amount of charge passing per unit area per unit time. The 'free' designation indicates currents not arising from bound charges in a dielectric or magnetic material, but from external sources like conductors. The SI unit is Amperes per square meter.

H.name: Magnetic Field Intensity
H.description: The magnetic field intensity vector, also known as the H-field. It is a vector quantity that describes the magnetic field generated by electric currents. It is related to the magnetic flux density \b{B} by \b{B} = \b{μH}, where \b{μ} is the permeability. The SI unit is Amperes per meter.
